name: Adept-2
baseline: CppAD (measured in the benchmark); autodiff (autodiff/autodiff, measured); ADOL-C and Sacado (named in the user guide, qualitative)
workload: Time to compute all sensitivities (reverse-mode adjoint AD) for four quant-finance workloads: Heston Monte Carlo (8 sensitivities), SABR calibration (15), XVA CVA (40), LIBOR swaption (161).
claimed_speedup: Gradient time, Adept vs CppAD: Heston MC 91 ms vs 268 ms; SABR calibration 19 ms vs 32 ms (autodiff 38 ms); XVA CVA 7.1 s vs 8.0 s; LIBOR swaption 1.15 s vs 4.57 s (about 2.9x, 1.7x, 1.1x, 4.0x, derived from page data). autodiff did not finish (DNF) on three of four workloads. XAD, the benchmark owner's own library, is faster than Adept in every row, so Adept is the second-fastest tape library there. The Adept user guide says reverse-mode differentiation 'tends to be significantly faster and use less memory' than ADOL-C, CppAD and Sacado, and usually only a little slower than a hand-written adjoint (no numbers in the guide; numbers are in Hogan 2014, ACM TOMS 40, 26).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on all libraries, median of 10 measured iterations after warmup (ad-benchmarks README)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Ubuntu 24.04
license: Apache-2.0 (library); GNU all-permissive license for test and benchmark code
stars_or_usage: 189 stars; used in climate and weather codes (ECMWF)
tradeoffs: Operator-overloading AD with expression templates; Adept 2 adds array classes and optimizers; autotools build; reverse mode records a tape; optimized BLAS recommended for matrix work.
caveats: The A-tier benchmark is run and published by Xcelerit, the vendor of XAD (a competing library that wins every row), so it is a competitor's benchmark of Adept; ADOL-C and Sacado are not in it. The original claim is in the peer-reviewed Hogan 2014 ACM TOMS paper, which I could not open here (the user guide at doc/adept_documentation.tex only states it qualitatively); verifiers should open that paper for the 2014 numbers. The Adept margin over CppAD is small on XVA CVA (7.1 s vs 8.0 s). Last upstream commits are small additions (Oct 2025).

name: HyperJet (hyper-dual number automatic differentiation)
baseline: Eigen AutoDiffScalar (nested), autodiff (dual2nd) and ceres::Jet
workload: Value, gradient and dense Hessian of a cable strain-energy sum (n = 3, 6, 12, 24 variables), median ns per evaluation over 7 repetitions with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Second order, static size: HyperJet 101 ns vs Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested 328 ns and autodiff dual2nd 375 ns at n=6 (3.3x vs the faster of the two); 921 vs 2888 and 2425 ns at n=12 (2.6x); 12,214 vs 22,105 and 17,679 ns at n=24 (1.5x); 15 vs 18 and 127 ns at n=3 (1.2x). First order (gradient only) there is no winner: HyperJet 244 ns vs AutoDiffScalar 245 ns vs ceres::Jet 304 ns at n=24.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG (Release CMake build; benchmark verifies identical values, gradients and Hessians before timing)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, macOS 26.5; Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0
tradeoffs: Header-only C++23 (Python bindings via pybind11); the fast variant needs the variable count at compile time, while the dynamic-size variant is 1.9x to 43x slower than the static one in the README's own text and, in its second-order table, is slower than both Eigen AutoDiffScalar and autodiff dual2nd at every size tested (n=3 to 24).
caveats: Author-run benchmark (first-party) on a single Apple Silicon machine, but the benchmark code is in the repository and the README is candid that there is no gain for gradient-only work. The Eigen baseline is AutoDiffScalar from Eigen's unsupported module, not Eigen Tensor. The README notes inlining decisions change absolute times by about 1.6x and that the benchmark forces inlining uniformly. Small project (17 stars).

name: Sleipnir
baseline: CasADi 3.8.0 (autodiff and NLP frontend) with Ipopt 3.14.20 and MUMPS 5.8.1
workload: Optimal-control NLP scalability benchmarks (flywheel with 100-5000 samples, cart-pole with 100-300 samples): problem setup time and solve time of Sleipnir's reverse-mode autodiff plus interior-point solver versus CasADi plus Ipopt.
claimed_speedup: Flywheel (ratios derived from page data CSVs): at 1000 samples solve 11.088 ms vs 59.015 ms (about 5.3x) and setup 0.368 ms vs 19.184 ms; at 5000 samples solve 75.124 ms vs 339.385 ms (about 4.5x) and setup 1.961 ms vs 91.157 ms. Cart-pole: setup 2.147 ms vs 194.851 ms at 300 samples, but solve is NOT faster there (2683.45 ms vs 1251.01 ms at 300 samples).
compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810; the root CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo; explicit -O flags are not listed in the benchmark README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7840U, 64 GB DDR5-5600
tradeoffs: C++23 with Python bindings; pool-allocated expression-node reverse-mode autodiff that records linearity to cache constant derivatives; uses Eigen sparse solvers; the NLP DSL picks the solver from problem structure. It is an AD-plus-NLP-solver stack, not a general tensor autodiff library.
caveats: Compares a full AD plus interior-point stack against CasADi plus Ipopt plus MUMPS, so AD speed alone is not isolated; CasADi uses tuned options (expand=true etc.) while Sleipnir uses defaults. Sleipnir's cart-pole solve times are slower than CasADi from 150 samples up (for example 3065.18 ms vs 973.846 ms at 250 samples; the Sleipnir cart-pole CSV has no 200-sample row), possibly because of different iteration counts. Flags are implied by the RelWithDebInfo default rather than listed, so tier A is borderline. Author's own benchmark; commercial linear solvers could change Ipopt's numbers.

workload: End-to-end CNN inference time in ms (VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-50, SqueezeNet, MobileNet, DenseNet-121) on ARM CPUs: Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72), iPhone 7, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3.
claimed_speedup: Huawei D05, best thread count, vs Caffe2+Eigen: VGG-16 12.84x, GoogleNet 4.45x, ResNet-50 2.29x, SqueezeNet 1.25x, MobileNet 2.65x; vs Caffe+OpenBLAS: VGG-16 10.86x, GoogleNet 13.7x, ResNet-50 3.88x, SqueezeNet 1.68x, MobileNet 4.03x, DenseNet-121 3.08x. VGG-16 on iPhone 7: 284 ms (2 threads) vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms. TX2 VGG-16 at 1 thread: 1325 ms vs Caffe2+NNPACK 5876 ms (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
hardware: Huawei D05 (Hi1616, 2x32 Cortex-A72 @ 2.40 GHz), iPhone 7 (A10 Fusion), Galaxy S8, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3B
tradeoffs: Loads Caffe models converted to its own .feathermodel format; targets ARM CPUs on iOS, Android and embedded or ARM-server Linux; small library with no external dependencies.

Baselines are 2018-2019 versions (Caffe2+Eigen scales badly at high thread counts, which inflates ratios such as 12.84x); speedups are computed from the best thread count; TVM on RK3399 (1293 ms) beat FeatherCNN at 2 threads (1420 ms); some wiki table cells are blank or unlabeled; compiler flags are not stated. hardware: AMD Ryzen 7950X (AVX2); Apple M2-Max (ARM NEON)

caveats: Author's own comparison in a GitHub discussion, no compiler or flags stated, discussion date not captured; mainline llama.cpp has kept improving, so the ratios are against the mainline of that time. README only says 'in many cases, better performance' and 'much faster CPU prompt processing for all non-interleaved quants'. Fork with substantial performance-relevant kernel changes (new GEMM/GEMV kernels, interleaved quants, FlashMLA).

The baseline is FP16 PyTorch matmul, which the plot labels as calling CUTLASS, not cuDNN or cuBLAS directly, and the headline compares 4-bit weights to 16-bit weights, so part of the speedup is the memory-traffic saving of quantisation rather than a faster FP16 kernel. The benchmark is by the RTNeural author, on one x86 Mac, with prebuilt ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite binaries and no stated compiler flags; layers are tiny, so per-call framework overhead dominates the baselines, and the advantage shrinks as layer size grows (STL backend falls to about the ONNX Runtime level at size 64 for GRU/LSTM). name: blip_mp
baseline: GMP 6.3.0 (mpz_t; built with assembly and with --disable-assembly)
workload: Own bench executable (blip_mp_bench) timing add/sub/mul/divMod/powm/invMod on pre-built pools of values at sizes from i64-range up to 98304 bits, e.g. 5M iterations of r = pool[i % 256] + pool[(i+1) % 256], against mpz_* in a C program using the same libc malloc.
claimed_speedup: On Apple Silicon: all i64-fitting values 1.95-2.66x faster than GMP; RSA 1024/2048/3072-bit mul 1.19-1.45x; RSA-2048 mul 1.16x, divMod 1.31x, powm 1.11x (README also says 13% faster powm at RSA-2048, 21% at 1024-bit); add at 768 bits and up 1.04-1.28x; sub at 256 bits and up 1.03-2.11x; 2048/1024-bit long division 24% faster. Loses to GMP-with-asm on x86_64 (GMP asm is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP-noasm on Zen 4) and on 128-bit add/sub, 16384+ bit multiply (0.55-0.87x) and modular inverse (2.5-4x behind).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast for blip_mp; GMP 6.3.0 from nixpkgs compiled with clang -O3; libc malloc for both; built with `nix build .#bench`
hardware: Apple M4 (aarch64-darwin, macOS 26.x) headline; cross-check on AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4, ~5.0 GHz boost) under NixOS
tradeoffs: Variable-length self-describing byte storage with small-buffer optimization instead of limb arrays; pure Zig, no inline assembly, C FFI exists. Integers only (no mpf/mpq/mpfr). FFT multiplication is implemented but disabled because Toom-3 still wins in the supported range, so it falls behind GMP past ~16K bits. Win is specific to Apple Silicon: on x86_64 GMP's hand-written assembly beats it by 1.5-4x on large operands.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE all 404 on raw); README says 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)', so license is treated as unclear and usability is reference. Research-grade; numbers are single-run or 3-run hand medians on one machine, with no statistical sampling, and the bench is the author's own. The author reports the GMP asm advantage on aarch64 is about 0% on M-series, so the win partly reflects GMP's weaker arm64 tuning. Very new repo (first commit 2026-05-16), 1 star.

name: CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)
baseline: GMP 6.1.2 (OpenMP, 20-core Xeon)
workload: Batched fixed-size unsigned big-integer operations (add, sub, low multiply, Montgomery reduction, odd modular exponentiation, div/qr, sqrt, gcd, modular inverse) at 128 to 8192 bits, one CUDA cooperative group of 4/8/16/32 threads per number, versus GMP calls spread over 20 CPU cores with OpenMP.
claimed_speedup: README speed-up table, Tesla V100 vs Xeon E5-2698v4 (GMP+OpenMP), average over 128-8192 bits: add 77.4x, sub 77.1x, mul (low) 43.5x, mont_reduce 29.3x, powm_odd 21.4x, div_qr 14.4x, sqrt 11.3x, gcd 6.9x, mod inv 4.1x; per-size extremes: 128-bit add 174.3x, 128-bit mul (low) 172.9x, 8192-bit powm_odd 16.8x, 8192-bit mod inv 4.0x
compiler_and_flags: GPU side: nvcc -arch=sm_<arch> xmp_tester.cu -lgmp (perf_tests/Makefile, no explicit -O flag, nvcc defaults); CPU side: g++ gmp_tester.cc -lgmp -fopenmp (no -O flag in the Makefile); GMP 6.1.2 built by the user
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU vs Intel Xeon E5-2698v4, 20 cores at 2.2 GHz
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA (Kepler through Ampere targets in the Makefile). Fixed-size unsigned integers only, 32 to 32K bits in 32-bit steps, 4/8/16/32 threads per number, written inside CUDA kernels with a fixed number of bits per kernel. It pays off for large batches of independent numbers, not for one big number. No floating point, no arbitrary-size operands.
caveats: A GPU is compared with a 20-core CPU running GMP, so the ratios say a V100 beats one Xeon socket, not that the algorithms are better per core. The README table does not say whether host-to-device transfer time is included. Numbers date from the 2018 beta release (V100, GMP 6.1.2). The Makefile has no -O flag for the g++ GMP harness, though the work happens inside libgmp. gcd and modular inverse gains are small (about 2.5x to 8x per size). The README table is first-party, though perf_tests/ lets anyone reproduce it (make gmp-run, make <arch>, then xmp_tester).

name: libzahl
baseline: GMP (also TomsFastMath and LibTomMath)
workload: Per-function micro-benchmarks of integer operations (set, swap, neg, abs, bit operations, comparison, add, sub, multiply, square, string conversion, gcd and more) on operands of 1 to 4097 bits, run through translation layers in bench/ for each library.
claimed_speedup: STATUS file: zset, zswap, zbtest, zsave, zload, zneg(a,b), zabs(a,b), ztrunc(a,b,c), zbits, zcmpu 'always fastest'; zadd 'fastest after ~90 (clang), ~260 (gcc+musl), or ~840 (gcc+glibc)'; zsub 'always fastest'; zlsh 'not too fast anymore'; zrsh 'gmp is almost always faster'; zmul and zsqr 'slowest'; zgcd '21 % of gmp'
compiler_and_flags: libzahl built with gcc+glibc, gcc+musl and clang+glibc; other libraries with gcc+glibc; config.mk CFLAGS = -std=c99 -O3 -flto; no CPU extensions or assembly extensions used
hardware: Intel Core 2 Quad Q9300 (x86-64), Linux, 50 us timer slack, benchmark process pinned to one CPU
tradeoffs: C library with long-jump error handling, allocation caching and no thread safety. Wins on cheap and small-operand operations; multiplication, squaring and many derived operations (modular multiply, pow, primality test) were still the slowest, so it does not beat GMP on arithmetic-heavy work. Plain C code, no assembly.
caveats: Mixed result, not a general win over GMP: the STATUS file's own multiply and square rows say 'slowest'. Measured on a 2008 Core 2 Quad with no vector extensions, so modern GMP assembly paths (mulx, adx, AVX) are not represented. The GMP numbers come through the repo's translation layer (bench/libgmp.h) and the GMP version is not stated; STATUS notes GMP does no failure checking while libzahl does, and TomsFastMath has a compile-time size limit. Repository archived 2024-10-06, last commit 2022-07-20. The README itself gives no numbers.

name: dashu (dashu-int)
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div, gcd, hex conversion and small-value workloads, for operand sizes 10 to 10^4 bits, dashu-int versus ibig, num-bigint, malachite-nz and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: Small operands: ubig_add at 100 bits dashu 3.7 ns vs rug 21.9 ns; ubig_div at 100 bits 5.7 ns vs 32.4 ns; ubig_mul at 100 bits 22.6 ns vs 25.1 ns; ubig_gcd at 1000 bits 2.87 us vs 3.05 us. Report summary: dashu faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases (one/two-word integers, 2-6x lower per-value overhead than GMP). rug/GMP is faster from about 1000 bits (ubig_mul at 10^4 bits: rug 4.52 us vs dashu 12.76 us).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated (cargo bench default assumed); dashu-int 0.4.2, rug 1.30.0 (GMP 6.x)
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, no C API (a Python binding exists), so use from C++ needs FFI work. Inline small-integer representation avoids GMP's per-value heap allocation, which is where it wins; large operands use slower algorithms than GMP.
caveats: The report calls itself 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative' (one laptop, short measurement time). Bit-width sweep stops at 10^4 bits, so no large-operand comparison. The benchmark repo has 3 commits and 2 stars. A second independent suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) shows GMP-backed rug far ahead of dashu on large workloads: digits of e at 10M digits rug 2.788 s vs dashu 19.943 s; Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs dashu 26.224 s. Dashu descends from ibig; GitHub fork status not confirmed. Win is limited to small operands and gcd; optimisation profile unstated, so tier B not A.

name: ibig
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div at 10 to 10^4 bits, ibig 0.3.6 versus dashu, num-bigint, malachite-nz and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: At 10 bits: ubig_add ibig 1.8 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_sub 1.5 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_mul 2.1 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_div 1.5 ns vs 28.3 ns. At 10^4 bits GMP wins: ubig_mul rug 4.52 us vs ibig 12.69 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline small-integer representation; no subquadratic gcd (10-13x slower than dashu/malachite/rug at 10^4 bits), no C API.
caveats: Win over GMP is confined to one-word integers (about 10 bits in the sweep); from about 1000 bits rug is ahead. The benchmarked version is ibig 0.3.6 while the repository now requires rustc 1.95 and carries an ibig-old directory, so the current code may differ. In the second suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) ibig is far behind rug on large workloads (digits of e at 10M: rug 2.788 s vs ibig 20.673 s). Dashu, a fork of ibig, is reported as its own entry. Report self-described as non-authoritative.

name: LibBF (Fabrice Bellard)
baseline: GNU MPFR (mpfr_mul, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate: GMP 6.3 / MPFR 4.2)
workload: Correctly rounded floating-point multiplication, addition, division and square root at 53 to 300,000 bits of precision, reported as ns per 64-bit limb.
claimed_speedup: Multiplication at 300,000-bit precision: libbf 51.2 ns/limb vs MPFR (rug) 78.9 ns/limb (about 1.5x faster, derived from page data). Not faster at 53-256 bits (43.4 vs 15.6 at 53 bits), at 3,000 bits (13.0 vs 9.4) or at 30,000 bits (43.0 vs 35.3); add, div and sqrt are slower than MPFR at every size listed.
compiler_and_flags: libbf version 2025-06-03 prebuilt bftest, clang -O2; rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, GMP 6.3, MPFR 4.2) under rustc 1.96.1 --release
hardware: Apple M4, 32 GiB RAM, macOS 26.5
stars_or_usage: 19 stars (mirror); embedded in QuickJS for BigInt/BigFloat
tradeoffs: Small (about 90 KB compiled), no dependencies, SIMD-optimised NTT multiplication with near-linear running time, also decimal floats and IEEE semantics. Transcendental functions are much slower than MPFR (exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518 ns/limb).
caveats: Win is limited to multiplication at very high precision on one Apple M4; MPFR is faster at every other operation and size in the same report. Measured by the author of libbeef, a competing Rust port, using libbf's own bftest harness; libbf operands come from a run-length random generator with sizes uniform in [1, 2*prec] bits while rug used full-width operands, so the comparison is not perfectly like-for-like. libbf's own README calls it 'not the fastest library' and says about 4x slower than TachusPI on pi. The upstream site bellard.org/libbf was blocked, so the GitHub mirror (rurban/libbf, tarball releases with CI fixes) is cited; its last commit is 2025-08-19.

name: Malachite
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div, gcd, extended gcd and conversions for 10 to 10^4 bits, malachite-nz 0.9.1 versus dashu, ibig, num-bigint and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: Tiny operands only: at 10 bits ubig_add malachite 2.1 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_mul 3.0 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_gcd 8.5 ns vs 20.9 ns, ubig_gcd_ext 25.8 ns vs 53.7 ns. At large sizes rug wins: ubig_mul at 10^4 bits malachite 8.28 us vs rug 4.52 us; ubig_gcd_ext at 1000 bits malachite 3.40 us vs rug 3.18 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp; criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; optimisation profile not stated; malachite-nz 0.9.1, rug 1.30.0 (GMP 6.x)
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std; LGPL-3.0 (GitHub page lists LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0; -only/-or-later variant not confirmed). Parts derived from GMP, FLINT and MPFR. No C API, so C++ use needs FFI.
caveats: Malachite beats GMP only on one-to-two-word integers, where GMP's per-value allocation dominates. The same report tallies malachite as fastest in 27 of 205 cases versus rug 52, with rug ahead from about 1000 bits. The second suite (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, malachite 0.4.14 vs rug 1.24.1) has rug faster everywhere: digits of e at 10M digits rug 2.788 s vs malachite 3.689 s, Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs malachite 5.192 s. Malachite's own site (malachite.rs) could not be opened, so no first-party claim recorded. Report is self-described as non-authoritative.

name: GNU MPFR with CUDA/CGBN backend (gnu-mpfr-cgbn)
baseline: MPFR 4.2.1 scalar functions (GMP 6.3.0) on one CPU core
workload: Correctly rounded mpfr_mul, add, div, sqrt and fma on batches of 1 to 16384 operands at 128 to 65536 bits of precision, GPU batch interface (with PCIe transfer) and device-resident vectors, versus the plain scalar MPFR function in a loop.
claimed_speedup: Peak batch speedups at n = 1024: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. Device-resident at n = 16384: fma 284x at 8192 bits, mul 230x at 4096, div 157x at 16384, add 120x at 8192, sqrt 115x at 16384. A single operation is always slower on the GPU (launch floor about 6.5 us resident, 16 us with transfers); batch add never beats the CPU (<= 0.7x); div and sqrt above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Backend built with NVCCFLAGS -O3 -arch=$cuda_arch -Xcompiler -fPIC (set by configure --enable-cgbn); CPU baseline is the stock MPFR 4.2.1 / GMP 6.3.0 build, its flags are not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs at 2.41 GHz), CUDA 13.2; CPU baseline is 'one core, the same machine' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Results are bit-identical to MPFR (same correctly rounded value, ternary value and flags for all five rounding modes); without --enable-cgbn the library is plain MPFR. Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA. Precision above 65536 bits runs on the CPU, all results in one batch must share a precision, device calls are serialized on a mutex, and only mul/add/sub/div/sqrt/fma are offloaded.
caveats: Tier C because the CPU model is not stated (everything else is public: the cgbnbench code, GPU, CUDA, MPFR and GMP versions). The repository is a single initial commit on 2026-09-12 with 3 stars, so it has had no outside use yet. Baseline is one CPU core against a whole GPU. The tree is GNU MPFR 4.2.1 with a patch, not a GitHub fork. It builds on steleman/nvidia-cgbn, a fork of NVlabs/CGBN that adds signed integers, Ada/Blackwell support and sizes up to 256K bits but publishes no new speed numbers.

name: MPLAPACK (multiple-precision BLAS/LAPACK with double-double, quad-double and CUDA backends)
baseline: GMP (mpf) and MPFR backends of the same library, at their default 512-bit precision
workload: Rgemm (multiple-precision matrix-matrix multiply) with square matrices on a Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, double-double and quad-double backends (with and without OpenMP) versus the GMP and MPFR backends, plus a CUDA double-double Rgemm on A100/V100 GPUs.
claimed_speedup: Manual section 9 peaks for Rgemm: reference GMP 19 MFlops and 693 MFlops OpenMP; reference MPFR 11 MFlops and 390 MFlops OpenMP; reference quad-double 33 MFlops and 1.3 GFlops OpenMP; reference double-double about 365 MFlops and 11.2 GFlops OpenMP. Derived from page data: double-double OpenMP is about 29x MPFR and 16x GMP, quad-double OpenMP about 3.3x MPFR and 1.9x GMP. README: CUDA double-double Rgemm and Rsyrk reach about 450 GFlops on a V100. Benchmark logs in the repo show the A100-box CUDA double-double kernel at 486,829 MFLOPS (n = 562).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0 inside Docker (manual); example builds use g++ -O2, benchmark flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, 256 GB DDR4-3200; GPU runs on Tesla V100 / A100 (benchmark/results/2022 folders)
tradeoffs: Faster only by giving up precision: double-double is about 32 digits (106 bits) and quad-double about 64 digits (212 bits), while the GMP and MPFR runs use 512 bits. Needs the dd/qd formats' accuracy to be enough; the library keeps one API across binary64, binary128, FP80, dd, qd, GMP and MPFR backends.
caveats: Not an equal-precision comparison: the GMP/MPFR columns are 512-bit, the dd and qd columns are 106 and 212 bits, so the speedups mostly reflect hardware double arithmetic versus software bignum. The manual itself says double results 'are not competitive to OpenBLAS or Intel MKL'. The author notes MPFR is about twice as slow as GMP, possibly because of the C++ binding copies. First-party (arXiv user manual v2.0.1, 2022) numbers; the 2023-2026 releases were not re-benchmarked in what was read. last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/multiple-precision listing (Sep 30, 2026).

name: mr_blackwell (native Miller-Rabin GPU kernel)
baseline: GMP (CPU Miller-Rabin probable-prime test with GMP modular exponentiation)
workload: Base-2 Miller-Rabin probable-prime tests (Montgomery CIOS modular exponentiation, 4-bit fixed window, PTX carry chains) on 65536 random 683-bit candidates, RTX 5070 GPU versus the CPU/GMP prime-gap test on a Ryzen 9 8800X3D.
claimed_speedup: CPU (GMP) 13,700 PRP/sec versus v2d kernel 1,805,000 PRP/sec at 683 bits = 132x (README table); 295,000 PRP/sec = 21x at 1240 bits. In the prime-gap pipeline the kernel runs about 1,800,000 PRP/sec versus 13,700 for the CPU test.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_120 (Makefile), CUDA 12.9, Linux Mint; GMP version and CPU baseline build flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5070 (SM 12.0 Blackwell) versus AMD Ryzen 9 8800X3D
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; the README says it produced 60 prime-gap world records (as of 2026-05-05) through the sethtroisi/prime-gap pipeline

The CPU baseline is the prime-gap gap_test_simple program, whose thread count, GMP version and flags are not stated, so the 132x is a GPU-versus-CPU ratio that may be against one core. The commits page showed no history to WebFetch, so last_commit is the 'updated' date from the github.com/topics/montgomery-multiplication listing (May 5, 2026), not a verified commit date. Mixed outcome: division and several elementary functions (atan, exp, log, pow) are slower than libquadmath. Compiler flags and library versions are missing, so tier C. The FMA ratio (about 35x, derived from page data) mostly reflects a very slow libquadmath fma.

The README itself records that an earlier 2.1x was really 1.21x because the baseline ran rocBLAS's default kernel, and ties the investigation to ROCm/rocm-libraries issue 9985 (rocBLAS default solution losing to another solution in the same library), so the win depends on how well the native baseline is tuned. Written with AI assistance (commits co-authored by an AI assistant). Baseline rocBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.

name: PureBLAS.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build) and AOCL-BLIS (AMD's BLIS fork); the repo's gate is max(OpenBLAS, AOCL)
workload: Single-threaded Float64 and ComplexF64 BLAS 1-3 and LAPACK routines across sizes on three AMD microarchitectures (2619 op/size/machine cells), measured with ABBA-interleaved rounds at locked clock frequency and the median ratio reported.
claimed_speedup: README: about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL), single-threaded. Median PureBLAS/OpenBLAS ratios (Zen3/Zen4/Zen5) from bench/gen_table.md: gemm 1.17/1.08/1.23, potrf 1.11/1.46/1.49, geqrf 1.55/1.79/1.66, getrf 1.17/1.20/1.31, gesvd 1.30/1.27/1.30, syev 1.40/1.44/1.34. Versus AOCL (gen_table_aocl.md): gemm 1.06/1.08/1.07, potrf 1.72/1.37/1.20, geqrf 1.64/1.30/1.24. notes.md: gemm at n=4096 is 1.252/1.280/1.308 (Zen4/Zen3/Zen5) against the faster of OpenBLAS and AOCL.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (README requires Julia 1.13) with LLVM; benchmark is `taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench` with BLAS.set_num_threads(1) and frequency locking via bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (methodology.md); no extra compiler flags stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3), Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4), Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5); measured 2026-09-23 (bench/provenance.md)
tradeoffs: Pure Julia BLAS and LAPACK (about 36k lines) that derives block sizes from detected cache and vector sizes. Inside Julia it reroutes LinearAlgebra through libblastrampoline with PureBLAS.activate(). It can also build libpureblas.so (ILP64 BLAS symbols, embedded Julia runtime) via juliac --trim, which the README calls experimental; that route makes it linkable from C/C++/Rust. Single-threaded only (multithreading deliberately on hold). Singular vectors only for Float64 and complex.
caveats: All measurements are the author's, on AMD hardware only (no Intel), single-threaded, Float64/ComplexF64 only. The win over OpenBLAS is larger than over AOCL, and roughly 13% of cells are below the gate (listed in docs/src/notes.md; some trmm/trsm/solve cells are 0.78-0.94 of AOCL). About 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity and the methodology page says run-to-run noise moves the below-gate count by 10-15 cells per sweep. notes.md says large-n gemm uses Strassen-Winograd (1.2-1.4x at large n), which has weaker numerical error bounds than classical gemm. The OpenBLAS version and AOCL version are not stated in the pages read. Repository is days old (first visible commits 2026-09-26) with 0 forks and no external users.

Versus Accelerate the median ratio is 1.11x, with Zynum ahead in 100 of 168 cases (derived from page data) and behind on sgemm medians (0.93x).

Zynum appears to dispatch SME/AArch64 kernels while OpenBLAS 0.3.34 on M5 likely runs NEON kernels, which probably explains the 3.9x median sgemm gap; Accelerate (Apple's vendor BLAS) is the fairer comparator and Zynum is roughly even to slightly slower on sgemm/dgemm medians (0.93x and 0.99x of Accelerate's GFLOP/s). name: fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard)
baseline: Intel MKL dgemm
workload: Sequential square dgemm (N = 1000 to 7500) comparing MKL against Strassen and other fast matrix multiplication algorithms with 1 to 3 recursion levels; run times in ms, median of five trials, data checked into data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data: Strassen with 2 recursion levels takes 4836 ms vs MKL 5361 ms at N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 ms vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x); 3 levels 15561 ms at N=6000 (1.16x); 1.04x at N=2000. The PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README) reports better performance than MKL dgemm on a shared-memory machine.
compiler_and_flags: C++11 with OpenMP and Intel MKL; flags set in make.incs/make.inc.linux (not read)
hardware: NERSC Edison (data/README.md says all data was collected on Edison; sequential results should be scaled to 3.2 GHz because of Turbo Boost); CPU model not stated in the files read
tradeoffs: Code-generated implementations of Strassen, Bini (approximate) and many other fast algorithms for sequential and shared-memory parallel use, calling MKL for base cases; requires MKL. Fast algorithms have weaker numerical stability (README reports errors about 1e-14 to 1e-15 for exact algorithms and larger for approximate ones) and only win for large matrices.
caveats: The 1.11-1.16x figures are derived from raw timing files and exclude the approximate (Bini) algorithm, which is faster still but numerically lossy; some rows in the data are noisy (for example one-level Strassen at N=1000 takes 405.8 ms vs 108.2 ms for MKL). The speedup applies only to N of about 2000 and above, and the machine is a 2014-era supercomputer node, so the ratio against current MKL on modern CPUs is unknown. The paper itself (arXiv 1409.2908) could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked); the paper claim is from the README citation and a search snippet.

Double-float arithmetic is not equivalent to native FP64, and the README warns against it for pivoted LU and eigensolvers. Last commit is about five months old.

SPD solve (512 matrices, 1 RHS): fused compact solve 2-9x over LAPACKE_dposv at orders 8-48, 1.4-2.2x at 60-105, geometric mean 1.7x, level with MKL's compact pipeline (0.9-1.0x geomean).

hardware: '4-core AVX-512 container' (CPU model not stated)

name: Admiral

workload: Complex and real 1-D (19 lengths for the FFTW comparison, 61 for ducc0) and N-D (9 shapes for FFTW, 27 for ducc0) FFTs in float and double on a 16-core AVX-512 Xeon, timed with nanobench (min across repetitions) after an accuracy gate against a reference DFT.
claimed_speedup: At 1 thread beats FFTW_MEASURE by 1.34x (1-D) and 1.43x (N-D), both precisions pooled; vs ducc0 at 1 thread 2.18x (f64) / 2.70x (f32) on 1-D, 1.12x / 1.41x on 2-D, 1.60x / 1.67x on 3-D; at 16 threads vs ducc0 2-D 1.27x / 1.58x and 3-D 2.67x / 3.53x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, -march=native (CMake release preset; further flags not listed; sweep of 2026-08-24 per benchmark/README.md)
hardware: Intel Xeon w5-3435X (16 physical cores, AVX-512)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (earliest commit visible on the commits page: 2026-09-11)
tradeoffs: Needs C++20 (buildable at C++17 with -DADM_CXX_STANDARD=17); GCC 14+ or Clang 19+ recommended, older compilers generate worse code. Compile time is long (compiled codelets up to radix 64 via xsimd and poet). Default -march=native binaries are not portable. Three interfaces: C++, C and an FFTW-subset drop-in (<admiral/fftw3.h>). Any size and rank, float/double/long double; no wisdom files (cost model at effort::estimate, plan-time race at automatic). Threads stay serial below about 32k elements.
caveats: Benchmark is run by the library author, and the same author wrote the fft_bench shootout repo (DiamonDinoia/fft_bench), so that repo is not independent evidence. The headline FFTW figure pools 19 1-D lengths and 9 N-D shapes and both precisions. In the fft_bench plots (images only, no numbers in the README) Admiral is roughly tied with MKL and FFTW over much of the 1-D range single-threaded on Xeon Platinum 8362, EPYC 7742 and EPYC 9474F, with MKL ahead at small sizes on Intel and FFTW ahead at small sizes on AMD, Sleef ahead at large sizes on EPYC 9474F, and multi-threaded MKL clearly ahead for large 1-D on the Intel node; that README also marks its MKL-omp numbers for rome and genoa as invalid. 16-thread 1-D vs threaded ducc0 is mixed per benchmark/README.md (geomean 0.33x to 1.82x by size). Very new project (earliest visible commit 2026-09-11), and the README says much of the code and cost-model tuning was done with Claude and that the author does not claim the fastest FFT. The licence is permissive with an attribution clause and may not be on the OSI list.

name: dft_simd (vertical-SIMD FFTW codelets for batched short DFTs)
baseline: FFTW3 plan/execute API (single DFT per execute, aligned; also 8 per execute and transposed variants)
workload: Transform 2^24 (16.8 million) short waveforms on one core: 60-sample real-to-complex (AVX2) and a 1024-point codelet (AVX2 and AVX512); FFTW API calls versus FFTW genfft-generated codelets recompiled to run on AVX vectors holding 8 (or 16) different waveforms.
claimed_speedup: 2025 update, AMD EPYC 9474F single core: 60-sample AVX2 codelet 149 ms (fixed-stride variant 79 ms) vs FFTW_Aligned_One 858 ms (README: 10.8x for the best variant); 1024-sample AVX2 codelet 9,124 ms (fixed stride 7,270 ms) vs 12,136 ms (README: about 1.6x); 1024-sample AVX512 codelet 12,628 ms (fixed stride 10,610 ms) vs 24,657 ms (README: 2.3x). 2018 Xeon E5-2650 v4: AVX codelet 220 ms vs FFTW3 2,194 ms for 1 waveform per call (about 10x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists: -march=native -std=c++11 -O3 (the -O3 is added for Release builds); README names gcc 4.8.5 for the Xeon run and Apple LLVM 9.0.0 for the laptop run; compiler of the 2025 EPYC run not stated
hardware: AMD EPYC 9474F single core (2025 update); Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4; MacBook Pro Intel Core i5-5287U 2.9 GHz
tradeoffs: Only helps when many same-size small transforms are batched and the data can be laid out so each SIMD lane holds a different waveform (vertical layout). Codelets must be generated with FFTW's OCaml genfft and compiled in advance; code size grows as N log N; there is no planner for large sizes. GPL because it derives from FFTW genfft output.
caveats: The baseline is FFTW's general API on the same batch, not a hand-tuned FFTW batched SIMD path. FFTW version is not stated (MacPorts install on the laptop run). The original tests used only N=60; the author says conclusions depend on compiler and CPU. Build type must be Release for -O3 to apply. The 2025 table is the only one with the EPYC and has no compiler line.

name: go-fft
baseline: FFTW 3.3.11 (native C, FFTW_MEASURE, threads=1); also numpy.fft, scipy.fft (pocketfft) and gonum/dsp/fourier
workload: Steady-state (plan reused) complex 1-D, real 1-D and complex 2-D FFTs in float64 on an Apple M4 Max, ns/op and GFLOP/s, with go-fft's 2-D path using several goroutines and every reference single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: Not faster than FFTW in 1-D: lags 1.17x to 3.28x on complex 1-D rows (e.g. N=1,024 3,395 ns vs FFTW 2,127 ns). Faster only on the 2-D multicore rows: 256x256 208,437 ns vs 271,098 ns; 512x512 633,920 ns vs 1,247,215 ns; 1024x1024 2,784,623 ns vs 6,301,688 ns. Vs scipy.fft (pocketfft) complex 1-D: N=256 716 ns vs 2,302 ns; N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 4,470 ns; N=65,536 377,784 ns vs 499,500 ns (slower at N=1,048,576: 13.36 ms vs 8.04 ms). Report summary: at or above parity with FFTW on 3 of 24 ops and with gonum on 19 of 19; 'typically 3-5x on composite N' faster than gonum.
compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 darwin/arm64 (CGO=0 pure Go); FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle with NEON, plans FFTW_MEASURE threads=1; numpy 2.5.0 and scipy 1.18.0 pinned single-threaded
hardware: Apple M4 Max (12P+4E), macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, so not callable from C++ without a wrapper. Arbitrary lengths: mixed radix for 13-smooth lengths, Rader for primes whose N-1 is 7-smooth, large-prime convolution otherwise (BENCHMARKS.md shows FFTW ahead at primes 1,009 and 10,007 by 1.26x and 2.15x). AVX2 and NEON SIMD butterflies. Plan creation is far cheaper than FFTW_MEASURE (e.g. 14,808 ns vs 3,434,000 ns at N=1,024).
caveats: Does not beat FFTW on the single-threaded rows; the only wins are 2-D shapes where go-fft fans rows and columns across goroutines while FFTW, numpy and scipy are single-threaded, so the 2-D comparison is not apples-to-apples. The report states real 1-D transforms lag FFTW by 1.51x to 3.20x. Recent commits are co-authored by an AI assistant and the repo is a few months old (earliest visible commit 2026-06-20). The README attributes part of the scipy gap at small N to Python FFI overhead on the scipy side, so the scipy comparison there is not like-for-like. Listed mainly because it is a benchmark-backed pure-Go FFT that beats the Go incumbent gonum and, at some sizes, scipy.fft.

claimed_speedup: docs/related.rst: NFFT 'significantly slower and/or more memory-intensive than FINUFFT'; CMCL NUFFT 'much (up to 50x even for one thread) slower'; MIRT 'slower than FINUFFT for all tolerances smaller than 10^-1'; DUCC 'in some regimes is faster than ours'. Legacy cuFINUFFT README: up to 10x over CPU FINUFFT and up to 100x faster than other established GPU NUFFT codes.
compiler_and_flags: nufft-bench README: GCC 7.3.0 (NFFT built with GCC 6.4.0), CMCL rebuilt with -fPIC -Ofast -funroll-loops -march=native; FINUFFT flags not stated there
stars_or_usage: 445 stars; used through jax-finufft, python bindings and nifty-ls
tradeoffs: Solves a different problem from uniform FFT libraries: nonuniform points, a tolerance parameter, spreading kernel. Uses FFTW or DUCC for the inner uniform FFT, CUDA for the GPU path. C, Fortran, MATLAB, Python and Julia interfaces.
caveats: The tier B rests on the peer-reviewed 2019 paper cited in the README; the paper itself could not be opened here (arXiv and SFU hosts blocked), and the page cited gives only the quotes above. ahbarnett/nufft-bench (the benchmark harness) says MIRT's apply step beats all others in 1-D and 2-D, and MIRT precomputation is very expensive. Benchmarks date from 2018-2019. Baselines are not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT, and the category fit (NUFFT) is loose.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'FINUFFT github flatironinstitute benchmark faster than NFFT nonuniform FFT'; mcp github search_repositories 'nufft'; related.rst and nufft-bench README opened for the claims
WebSearch 'FINUFFT benchmark faster than NFFT github flatironinstitute nonuniform FFT library'; docs/related.rst and docs/nfft_migr.rst

name: PhastFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw crate); also RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex-to-complex forward and inverse FFT, f32 and f64, power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608, divan benchmark on an M1 MacBook Pro in a third-party benchmark repo (astral4/fft-benchmark).
claimed_speedup: f32 N=1024: 4.749 us (PhastFT) vs 7.291 us (FFTW) forward; f32 N=1,048,576: 10.21 ms vs 14.20 ms; f32 N=8,388,608: 109.0 ms vs 193.3 ms (RustFFT 103.9 ms). Third-party conclusion: 'phastft was the fastest in most tests, but rustfft was the fastest on the smallest and largest sequence lengths tested' and 'fftw was consistently slower than both rustfft and phastft'. Memory: 8.388 MB (PhastFT) vs 41.94 MB (RustFFT) at f32 N=2^20 (derived from page data, about 5x less).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (2024-05-03); phastft v0.2.1, rustfft v6.2.0, fftw crate v0.8.0 over FFTW 3.3.8 compiled with Apple clang 15.0.0; cargo profile and FFTW configure flags not stated
hardware: M1 MacBook Pro (exact variant not stated). PhastFT's own README plots use a MacBook Air with Apple M2, 4P+4E cores, 24 GB, multi-threaded.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two lengths only. Runtime SIMD selection (no -C target-cpu=native needed). In-place algorithm with much lower memory than RustFFT. Optional multi-threading through the 'parallel' feature. The 2024 benchmark used v0.2.1, which needed nightly Rust for portable SIMD; the current Cargo.toml says rust-version 1.88.
caveats: Independent but small personal benchmark repo from 2024 (not a well-known suite), Apple Silicon only, cargo flags not stated, single machine. The FFTW times look high for small N (about 1.4 us at N=8), which suggests the FFTW 3.3.8 build or the binding did not use NEON codelets or adds per-call overhead; treat the FFTW comparison on Apple Silicon with caution. RustFFT beats PhastFT at N<=32 and N>=2^22 (f32). PhastFT's own README benchmarks (M2, multi-threaded, vs RustFFT and FFTW3) are plots only, with no numbers in text.

The third-party README conclusion that FFTW 'was consistently slower' than rustfft is contradicted by its own f32 table at N=1024 to 16384 forward. name: FastAndFourier (FAF, JIT-compiled DSP/FFT library)
baseline: KissFFT (and FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE/FFTW_MEASURE, which beat it); also NotoriousFFT
workload: Single-transform C2C latency in double precision at N=8 to 65536, first on macOS x86_64 (2026-02-22) and then Linux aarch64 interleaved FP64 (2026-09-03).
claimed_speedup: x86_64 macOS, 2.3 GHz AVX2: at N=65536 907 us vs KissFFT 3253 us (README: 3.2-3.6x faster; 3.6x derived from page data) but slower at N=64 (4.40 vs 1.11 us), 1024 (75.3 vs 27.1 us) and 16384 (1595 vs 634 us); FFTW3 measure is 3-10x faster than everything. Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz: 53.8 ns vs 95.3 ns at N=8, 0.778 vs 0.850 at N=64, 16.5 vs 21.7 at N=1024, 2238 vs 2735 at N=65536 (slightly slower at N=16: 0.161 vs 0.149).
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops for the x86 run (README); -O3 -march=native for the aarch64 run; compiler name not stated
hardware: x86_64 2.3 GHz with AVX2 under macOS Ventura and Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz; CPU models not named
tradeoffs: Runtime JIT: transforms are lowered to C and compiled by a system C compiler (falls back to a VM interpreter without one). Sizes up to 2^16, 5-smooth sizes plus codelets and Rader primes, optional Bluestein. Part of a larger DSP library with a scripting language, DWT and CWT.

The README flags the x86 table as the old VM-floor result. First-party numbers, CPU models not named. NotoriousFFT, by the same author, is faster than FAF on aarch64 by 1.2-2.15x. baseline: FFTW 3 through the ezFFTW Java wrapper (single-threaded)

hardware: Not stated ('observations for my machine')

name: minfft
baseline: KissFFT
workload: One-dimensional double-precision in-place forward complex DFT of size N=2 to 2^20, speed in MFLOPS, plotted against KissFFT, PocketFFT and a machine-specific SSE2 FFTW (docs/speed.svg).
claimed_speedup: README says its speed and accuracy are compared with 'libraries of similar design - KissFFT and PocketFFT', with FFTW shown for reference; the plot has no numbers in text. Digitised from the data points of docs/speed.svg (derived from page data, approximate, axes log2(N) and MFLOPS): minfft is above KissFFT at every size, about 1.4x to 4.8x, median about 2.0x (e.g. N=2^10 about 8,200 vs 5,000 MFLOPS); about on par with PocketFFT (median about 0.9x, lower for N>=2^10) and about 0.55x of FFTW SSE2.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two lengths only, any dimensionality; complex and real DFT and DCT/DST types 2 to 4. Double precision by default (single via MINFFT_SINGLE). C89 and Fortran 2003 interfaces, in-place or out-of-place, auxiliary data object per plan. Split-radix (2/4) DIF algorithm, 'simple means' rather than hand-tuned SIMD; far slower than FFTW with SIMD.
caveats: First-party plot with no stated CPU, compiler or flags, and the ratios above were read from SVG coordinates, not from quoted numbers. It is not faster than PocketFFT at large sizes. The README plots are the only performance evidence found; a separate repo, NotoriousLOB/Notorious-FFT, reports its own header-only FFT beating minfft by 1.08x to 1.13x on an ARM Cortex-A78AE, which suggests minfft is a reasonable small-library reference but is not evidence for minfft's speed.

workload: Randomized interleaved Google Benchmark sweep, 90 iterations per scenario, taskset -c 2: 14 mixed 1-D sizes (4096 to 1048576 including primes and near-primes), five 2-D shapes (256x256 to 1024x1024) and four 3-D shapes (64^3 to 128x128x64); c2c, r2c and c2r. Ratio is other implementation CPU ns over tuned fork CPU ns.
claimed_speedup: SIMD build, median ratio (tuned wins/ratios): 1-D c2c 2.40x vs upstream PocketFFT (1258/1260), 1.35x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE (813/1260), 4.63x vs KissFFT (952/990), 3.25x vs meow_fft; 1-D r2c 2.50x and c2r 2.75x vs upstream, 1.45x and 1.44x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE; 2-D c2c 6.43x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE. Slower than FFTW_MEASURE (0.71x for 1-D c2c) and KFR (0.49x). 2-D and 3-D versus upstream PocketFFT are about 1.0x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the READMEs: benchmarks use CXX/CXXFLAGS from the Makefile environment; FFTW 3.3.10 built from the release tarball; KFR 7 built with clang++ C++20; SIMD and no-SIMD builds
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11 like PocketFFT; the tuning targets hot 1-D paths (large power-of-two c2c terminal stages, fused pass4x4, split8 buffering, measured dispatch for selected mixed radix). Keeps PocketFFT features (float/double/long double, multi-dimensional, DCT/DST, Bluestein).
caveats: First-party benchmark by the fork author. CPU model is not stated; the workstation was not quiet (ASLR on, load average often above idle) and the author calls the numbers a local snapshot. The fork loses to FFTW_MEASURE and KFR on most 1-D cases and to upstream on some 2-D/3-D cases. MKL is not in the harness. Fork changes performance-relevant code, so it is reported here, but the orchestrator may fold it under PocketFFT. Floating-point precision of the runs is not stated in the README.

name: SFFT3 (3-D FFT built from FFTW 1-D transforms)
baseline: FFTW3 own 3-D routines (FFTW_PATIENT on the Ryzen table, FFTW_MEASURE on the i7 table)
workload: Average time of a forward plus reverse 3-D real FFT from 64^3 to 2100x2100x121 (and 2048x2048x1024), one OpenMP thread per physical core, padding and planning time excluded; SFFT3 uses FFTW's 1-D routines with cache-blocked transposes and a per-thread workspace.
claimed_speedup: 8-core Ryzen 3700X: 512^3 8.428e-2 s vs FFTW3-P 1.009e-1 s (1.20x, derived from page data); 1024^3 7.733e-1 s vs 1.011 s (1.31x, derived); 256^3 1.112e-2 vs 1.213e-2 s; slower at 64^3 (1.821e-4 vs 1.185e-4 s) and 128^3. 4-core i7-6700K vs FFTW_MEASURE: 512^3 0.182 vs 0.196 s (1.08x, derived), 1024^3 1.640 vs 1.705 s (1.04x, derived), slower at 128^3 and 2100x2100x121.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version and optimization flags not stated in the README); i7 run built with CFLAGS=-DSFFT3_L2=256000
hardware: 8-core AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (Ubuntu 24.04.2); 4-core Intel i7-6700K (Ubuntu 22.04.5)
tradeoffs: Not an independent FFT: it calls FFTW3 for every 1-D transform (GPL). Uses a larger workspace than FFTW's 3-D plans (author says timings are not directly comparable). No explicit vectorization, no auto-tuning; L1/L2 sizes are compile-time constants.
caveats: Author calls it an untested proof-of-concept run on two similar machines and expects the results not to generalize; wins are 4-31% on large cubes and it loses at small sizes. Compiler version, flags and FFTW version are not stated.

name: detria
baseline: CDT (artem-ogre/CDT) and poly2tri; Triangle (CMU) is also in the comparison but is faster on random point sets

claimed_speedup: Medians printed in the per-case SVG result files (images/benchmark/*.svg, embedded in BENCHMARKS.md; detria vs CDT vs Triangle, ms): world land outline (407,072 vertices) 502 vs 1431 vs 441; United States outline 24.4 vs 58.8 vs 27.2; Afghanistan (1,532 vertices) 0.74 vs 2.17 vs 0.87; 10,000-vertex debug2.dat 11.6 vs 28.7 vs 12.5. Tallied over the 23 result files: faster than CDT in 21 of 23 cases (about 1.5x to 3.2x), faster than poly2tri in all 14 cases it supports, faster than Triangle in 16 of 23 (country outlines, city.dat, debug2.dat). Slower than Triangle on random points (1,000,000 points: 1798 vs 946 ms) and the world land outline (502 vs 441 ms), and slower than both Triangle and CDT on the cocircular fractals of depth 6 and 8 (depth 8: 3091 vs 1407 CDT vs 857 Triangle).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17.0.3 (MSVC-like command line), release build with default compiler flags
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Single-header CDT with a C# port; no point insertion after triangulation, no Steiner or refinement (stated non-goal). CDT and poly2tri versions are not stated. Triangle is still faster for generic point sets.

The A tier rests on 'default compiler flags' of a release build, which is vague. Baseline versions are not stated, the machine is a 2019 desktop on Windows, and neither CDT nor poly2tri is the category's incumbent (CGAL, Boost.Geometry, GEOS are not compared).

name: geo-utils-cpp
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 (spherical_equatorial strategy: bg::within and bg::area); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7

workload: Validation and repair (ST_MakeValid equivalent) of 1,579,030 polygon parts from a production GeoPackage, plus synthetic cases (valid polygons, bowties, collapsed rings, near-collinear, large coordinates, linestrings) of 4 to 10,000 vertices; parallel batch.
claimed_speedup: Real-world dataset (README): validation 2.1 s (1.3 us/poly) vs GEOS 3.0 s (1.9 us/poly), 1.4x; full pass 3.6 s vs 3.0 s (0.83x, GEOS faster). docs/BENCHMARKS.md table: validation 2.47 s vs 3.46 s (1.40x), full pass 4.05 s vs 3.49 s (0.86x). Synthetic: valid polygon 4v 4.8x, invalid bowtie 4v 25x, bowtie 1000v 8.0x, collapsed 1000v 5.5x, zero-length line 45x. GEOS faster on large valid polygons (10000v 0.37x), spaghetti (0.56x) and large coordinates 1e12 (0.08x at 1000v).

hardware: Intel i5-12400F (6C/12T), Windows 10
tradeoffs: Specialised to geometry validation and repair, not a general GEOS replacement. Rayon parallel batch API; Structure strategy mirrors GEOS ST_MakeValid, Arrange strategy is a CDT fallback. Built-in WKB/WKT/batch I/O. Passes the GEOS XML validation suite per README.
caveats: Mixed results: GeoRepair loses on large valid polygons, spaghetti geometry, large coordinates and on the full real-world pass. GeoRepair column is a 12-thread Rayon batch while GEOS is serial per call driven concurrently via Rayon in the same process. README history note: earlier GEOS columns went through a WKT round trip that inflated wins 30-500x; the current harness builds geometry directly. First-party benchmark. Sub-microsecond rows are dispatch noise per the authors.

claimed_speedup: cmpute suite (Ubuntu 20.04 WSL2): 100,000 boxes insertion 0.195 ms/box (Boost) vs 0.876 ms/box (libspatialindex) and 0.443 ms/box (SQLite R*Tree), i.e. about 4.5x and 2.3x (derived from page data); query at 10,000 boxes 0.0217 ms/box vs 0.2852 and 0.6142 (about 13x and 28x, derived); file size after shrink 6.19 MB vs 25.8 MB and 8.5 MB. mloskot suite (values read off README charts, approximate): bulk-loaded R* 1M objects about 1.1 s (bgi) vs about 5.5 s (libspatialindex STR); 100K intersection queries on the bulk-loaded tree about 0.05-0.12 s vs about 2-6 s; iterative R* load of 1M objects about 3-13 s vs about 25-108 s depending on node capacity.
compiler_and_flags: mloskot: Visual C++ 11.0 (Visual Studio 2012) 32-bit build, flags not stated; cmpute: not stated
hardware: mloskot: Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.10GHz, 16 GB RAM, Windows 7; cmpute: Ubuntu 20.04 on WSL2, CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Header-only, requires Boost headers; compile-time or run-time node parameters; bulk loading; persistent storage only through memory-mapped files, which are not dynamically sized.
caveats: Boost.Geometry is itself one of this category's named incumbents, so this entry only claims its R-tree beats libspatialindex and SQLite R*Tree. The cmpute repo is archived (last commit 2021-04-22), has no license file, 2 stars, and does not state compiler, flags or CPU; the mloskot repo (last commit 2019-07-07, authors include a Boost.Geometry.Index author) calls itself a non-academic first prototype with possible bugs. The cmpute note says mmap storage is not strictly file-based. Old library versions; the mloskot numbers are chart read-offs. Query checksums in the cmpute logs differ between libraries, so result equality was not demonstrated.

Arcs kept exactly vs Clipper at 1e-2: 76.4x on the circle (0.12 vs 9.47 ms), 84.9x on PathologicalProfile1/10 (1.61 vs 136.46 ms), 15.8x on PathologicalProfile1/100 (85.10 vs 1347.09 ms). Against Clipper at 1e-3: up to 494.7x on the circle and 861.0x on PathologicalProfile1/10.

Numbers: construction geo-index hilbert 80.891 ms vs rstar bulk 159.34 ms; STRTree 116.52 ms; search 116.41 us (flatbush-style) vs rstar 153.62 us; with the rayon feature STRTree construction drops to 72.099 ms.

name: pgl (Pangolin plane geometry library)

workload: Wall-clock time of 2D computational-geometry problems (triangulation, convex hull, kd-tree/AABB search, segment intersection, arrangements, polygon unions, Minkowski sum, visibility) on identical integer-coordinate inputs, pgl number type vs the comparable CGAL kernel, across input sizes up to the dataset limits (random data plus Salzburg polygon database).

ERational vs EPECK: segment intersection 0.55x (0.19-1.8), regularized union of triangles 0.23x (0.20-0.59), arrangement point-location query 0.46x (0.32-0.84), segment search count in Rectangle 0.68x, nearest neighbor query 0.82x. int vs EPICK: segment search count in Triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x, count in Rectangle 0.51x, convex hull 0.51x. CGAL is faster on Delaunay triangulation (pgl 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK, 1.7x slower int/EPICK), triangulation point location, Minkowski sum and kd-tree build. Overall ERational/EPECK spans CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; int/EPICK spans CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.

Some rows favor pgl by construction (CGAL Kd_tree has no triangle query, so the benchmark wrote one). Ratios are averaged over two machines. name: qdgeo
baseline: GEOS 3.13.1 (via Shapely 2.1.2): union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and buffer
workload: 26 boolean/buffer workloads over a 4,040-parcel, 135,080-coordinate public county parcel dataset (GeoMoose demo data); each figure is median of three suite runs of 11 repeats.
claimed_speedup: README: full-dataset parcel union is 3.1x native GEOS (qdgeo wasm 160 ms, qdgeo native 130 ms vs GEOS 426 ms for 4,040 parcels; 1,000 parcels 20.3 / 16.8 ms vs 65.7 ms). Geometric mean over the 26 workloads: GEOS native 1.5x slower than qdgeo wasm (range across runs 1.36-1.62). Buffer of 100 parcels +2 m: 1.30 ms vs GEOS 4.54 ms. GEOS is faster on a single 19,208-coordinate parcel buffer (8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe (shipped build keeps safety checks); WASM build run in Node 22+
hardware: One idle machine; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Only five operations (four booleans and rounded buffer). Rejects invalid geometry instead of repairing it, and valid input can occasionally fail (4 of 3,946 cluster unions) because it declines to snap coordinates. WASM artifact 135 KB raw, 50.8 KB gzipped, no C or C++ dependency; Zig native build has a C-compatible ABI.
caveats: Application-level comparison: the README admits boundaries are not equal. GEOS runs on already-built geometry objects via shapely.union_all (no parse/encode) while qdgeo rows include WKB codec cost, which favors GEOS; but GEOS is native and qdgeo also reports a native column. The README says to treat gaps under 20% as unresolved. GEOS is faster on very large single polygons. Project is days old. Not a general GEOS replacement. CPU model missing so tier C.

workload: Time per sample (ns) to generate 1 million standard-normal samples (min of 10 trials) in single and double precision; each algorithm is in its own file and all but cpp11random use a simple LCG as the uniform source.

Ziggurat is Jochen Voss's implementation. The results list SIMD variants only for single precision.

The CLT variants fail the repo's own kurtosis check. Single 2012-era CPU and a 2015 toolchain. Compiler version and flags were inferred from a result file name and the premake script rather than the README text, so the tier could be argued as B.

name: ra_prng / ra_core (array-based addressable PRNG)
baseline: xoshiro256** (also Philox4x32-10, ChaCha20 and /dev/urandom)
workload: bench_release.c on one pinned core: seed-plus-generate cost for batches of K=1 and K=255 words per key (reinit on every call) and for long streams, ns per word.
claimed_speedup: ra_core_singleblock K=255: 0.191 ns/word (20018 MB/s) vs xoshiro256** 1.30 ns/word (2937 MB/s) and Philox4x32-10 3.79 ns/word; README states about 6.8x faster than xoshiro256** and 19.9x faster than Philox in that regime. K=1: 1.13x faster than Philox but 1.77x slower than xoshiro256**. ra_core_orbit long stream: 3.87 ns/word vs xoshiro256** 1.20 ns/word (about 3.2x slower).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0, -O3 -march=native, pinned with taskset -c 0, min of 5 to 7 trials plus best of 8 outer runs (benchmark file experiments/2026-9-1_family-productionization/bench_release.c).
hardware: Intel Core i3-1115G4, Arch Linux 6.8.7
tradeoffs: About 2 KB state (two 256-entry arrays that permute each other); random-access addressable initialization (key + addr_hi); wins only for many short batches that reseed, loses to xoshiro256** for continuous streams; no SIMD or GPU version; not cryptographic; Python bindings compile with -march=native at install.
caveats: Very new repo (first commit 2026-08-25); the commit history lists an AI assistant as co-author. The README admits an earlier 30303 MB/s claim was not reproducible and that a benchmark fairness bug (inlining of reference baselines) was found and fixed on 2026-09-12. Self-reported only; the 'accepted but unpublished' paper could not be checked. CC BY-NC-SA is non-OSI and non-commercial, so the code must not be copied.

name: simdrng (SIMD Xoshiro256++, ChaCha and Philox generators)
baseline: scalar xoshiro256++ (reference), std::uniform_real_distribution, and std::mt19937_64
workload: Google Benchmark on CI: u64 buffer fill of 4096 values and single-value calls for scalar vs xsimd-dispatched generators, double generation via uniform() vs std::uniform_real_distribution, and std::mt19937_64 single-value calls.
claimed_speedup: Benchmark JSON (gcc-15): XoshiroSIMD fill_u64 1645 ns per 4096 values (about 2.49e9 values/s) vs scalar Xoshiro fill_u64 3835 ns (about 1.07e9 values/s), about 2.3x (derived from page data); scalar Xoshiro uniform() 1.32 ns vs std::uniform_real_distribution 4.65 ns (about 3.5x, derived from page data); std::mt19937_64 single u64 call 1.60 ns. docs/benchmarks.rst: 'Xoshiro reaches ~2.3x its scalar loop' in bulk fill and uniform() 'roughly 3x' faster than std::uniform_real_distribution.
compiler_and_flags: gcc-15 (also gcc-14, clang-19, clang-20 result directories); CMake Release with the 'bench' preset (-march=x86-64-v3) and xsimd runtime dispatch
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (cpu_model.txt; GitHub-hosted runner, Google Benchmark reports 4 CPUs at 2445 MHz)
tradeoffs: C++20, needs xsimd and poet (single-header branch available); each SIMD generator keeps a 256-value (2 KiB for u64) output buffer, so state is larger and single-value calls are slower than scalar xoshiro. Python bindings (nanobind, numpy.random.Generator compatible) included. Philox and ChaCha variants are scalar, SIMD-dispatch and -march=native builds.
caveats: The gain is for bulk fills only: single-value SIMD calls cost 2.82 ns vs 0.94 ns for scalar Xoshiro, so a one-value-at-a-time loop is slower than the baseline. The mt19937_64 figure is a per-call time, not a bulk-fill figure, so it is not directly comparable to the fill numbers. Numbers come from a shared CI runner. License is BSD-3-Clause with an added acknowledgement clause (clause 4); that SPDX id is not on the OSI-approved list as far as I know, so usability is marked reference although the text is permissive; the orchestrator may want to reclassify. Comparison against std::mt19937_64 in bulk was not measured.

name: VMT19937 (V-family and X-family vectorized Mersenne Twister)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (the 'STL-MT19937-64' rows); also the original reference MT19937 / SFMT19937 and Intel MKL MT/SFMT
workload: Throughput in million samples/s of 32-bit (MT19937, SFMT19937) and 64-bit (MT19937-64) random numbers, about 1.6e10 numbers per CPU (30 runs of 8.19e6 samples), in scalar (one value per call) and vectorial (block of 10,240) query modes, on five CPU targets (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE256).
claimed_speedup: README table, M samples/s, vectorial mode: V-MT19937-64 2865 (AVX-512) / 1161 (AVX2) vs STL-MT19937-64 590 / 317 (about 4.9x and 3.7x, derived from page data); V-MT19937 2392 (AVX2) vs ORIG-MT19937 259 (about 9.2x, derived from page data); V-SFMT19937 10943 (AVX-512) vs ORIG-SFMT19937 4445 (about 2.5x, derived from page data). Scalar mode: X-MT19937-64 1095 (AVX-512) vs STL 590 (about 1.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16 per doc/main.tex; Makefile default is -O3 -std=c++20 with -march=native on x86 (-march=armv8-a+simd on NEON, -march=armv8-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=256 on SVE); the bench harness is perf.exe built by the repo Makefile.
hardware: Intel Celeron J4125 2.0 GHz (SSE4.2), Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (AVX2), Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C 2.9 GHz (AVX-512), Neoverse-N1 2.5 GHz (NEON), Neoverse-V1 2.6 GHz (SVE256) (from doc/main.tex).
tradeoffs: The V-family changes the output sequence: it interleaves several MT19937 states de-phased by polynomial jump-ahead, and the sequence depends on the chosen register width (VRegBitLen). The X-family is bit-identical to the original MT19937/MT19937-64/SFMT sequences. Needs jump-polynomial data files (dat/poly) for the V-family, C++20, and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON/SVE hardware for the large gains. Large block-fill API (block of 16 or state-size blocks) is where the speedup is.
caveats: Big speedups are in vectorial (block fill) mode; scalar single-value V-MT19937 is only about 1.7-2.1x the original reference. Intel MKL-MT is faster than V-MT19937 at AVX-512 vectorial (6479 vs 5742 M/s). The STL row exists only in the MT19937-64 table, so 32-bit std::mt19937 is not measured directly (the ORIG-MT19937 reference is the baseline there); on SVE256 STL-MT19937-64 (573) beats V-MT19937-64 scalar (513). Which standard library built the STL rows is not stated. First-party results from a single author; paper arXiv 2309.16682 could not be opened (egress blocked). CPU models and 'GCC 16' were read from the LaTeX source doc/main.tex, not the README. All ratios are derived from page data.

WebSearch: 'github VMT19937 SIMD-friendly Mersenne Twister vectorized implementation AVX-512 code'; opened the repo page, README.md, BUILD.txt, Makefile and doc/main.tex.

name: vphilox (SIMD Philox4x32-10 counter-based engine)
baseline: std::mt19937 (PCG64 and xoshiro256++ in the same table)
workload: Cost per byte (RDTSC reference cycles) of bulk generate_n and per-value operator() relative to std::mt19937 on the same machine, five CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Cost relative to std::mt19937 (lower is faster), generate_n: 0.75x Raspberry Pi 5 NEON, 0.38x Sapphire Rapids, 0.22x Skylake-SP, 0.24x Cascade Lake 4 vCPU, 0.33x Cascade Lake 32 vCPU. Same machines, PCG64: 0.83x, 0.59x, 0.33x, 0.32x, 0.53x; xoshiro256++: 0.28x, 0.30x, 0.24x, 0.17x, 0.29x. README: buffer fill runs at 1.3x to 4.6x the throughput of std::mt19937; vphilox beats xoshiro256++ only on Skylake-SP (0.4210 vs 0.4703 cycles/byte).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) in the Skylake-SP and Sapphire Rapids environment files; CMake 'bench' preset (Release, full optimization), exact flags not opened. Raw JSON and environment files are in results/.
hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 (NEON); Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C (Sapphire Rapids); Intel Xeon 2.00GHz family 6 model 85 stepping 3 (Skylake-SP, 4 vCPU GCP); Cascade Lake (family 6 model 85 stepping 7) on a 4-vCPU slice and a 32-vCPU two-socket host.
tradeoffs: C++20 header-only. Counter-based Philox with bit-exact output across compilers, OSes, CPUs and thread counts, O(1) discard/seek, text checkpoint save/restore, per-thread streams without locks. AVX-512, AVX2, NEON and scalar backends. Use generate_n for the speed; per-value operator() costs 0.51x to 1.15x of std::mt19937. Slower than xoshiro256++ on four of five CPUs.
caveats: Very new, one author, not yet tagged, no stars. All numbers are first-party. Cycles per byte uses RDTSC reference cycles and is only comparable inside one machine. Per-value drawing on Pi 5 is 0.87x the speed of std::mt19937. Compiler details were only checked on two x86 environment files. libstdc++ inferred from GCC on Linux.

name: FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers and shuffle)
baseline: std::shuffle (libstdc++ as of the paper, divide-based uniform_int_distribution) and OpenBSD-style / Java-style bounded-random algorithms
workload: Shuffling arrays of 32-bit and 64-bit elements, sizes 5 to 1e9, nanoseconds per array element, every variant, including std::shuffle through a UniformRandomBitGenerator wrapper, draws from the same lehmer64 generator (cpp/shuffle.cpp).
claimed_speedup: Sample results.txt in TOMACS_RCR/README.md, array size 10000, 32-bit indexes: nearly divisionless 1.80 ns/element vs OpenBSD-like 5.32, Java-like 2.98, std::shuffle 18.57 (std::shuffle about 10x slower, derived from page data); 64-bit indexes: 1.78 vs 14.40, 7.97 and 15.23 (std::shuffle about 8.6x slower, derived). README notes the exact numbers will vary.
compiler_and_flags: g++ or clang++ with -std=c++11 -O3 (cpp/Makefile); compiler version not stated.
hardware: Not stated (README shows sample output only; advises Linux, TurboBoost and hyperthreading off).
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; algorithm adopted by libstdc++, Abseil, Swift, Go, Julia, Zig and NumPy per the README
tradeoffs: Benchmark and experiment code for Lemire's multiply-and-reject method (needs 128-bit multiply; 'nearly divisionless'), not a packaged library. The idea is easy to copy into any PRNG wrapper.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (ACM TOMACS 2019, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval') with a replication package, but the numbers on the page are an illustrative sample run and the CPU is not stated. The std::shuffle baseline reflects libstdc++ before it adopted this very technique, so the gap against a current libstdc++ is smaller. The benchmark generator is lehmer64, not std::mt19937, so the std::shuffle column isolates the range-reduction cost.

name: MELG-64 (maximally equidistributed Mersenne-prime-period generators)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers; MELG19937-64 vs MT19937-64, MT19937-64 (ID3) and SFMT19937-64 (with and without SIMD).
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: MELG19937-64 4.2123 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s (about 1.21x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 6.2920 s vs 6.6490 s (about 1.06x, derived from page data). README calls it 'speeds equivalent to 64-bit Mersenne Twisters'; its main point is Delta=0 (maximally equidistributed) vs 7820 for MT19937-64.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the README; build line 'gcc melg19937-64.c -o melg19937-64 -O3 -Wall')
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 15 stars; ACM TOMS 2018 paper (Harase and Kimoto) cited in the README

caveats: The speed gain over MT19937-64 is modest (about 6-21%) and SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is much faster (1.8457 s and 2.8806 s); the value is equidistribution quality, not raw speed. Peer-reviewed paper cited but not opened; whether the timing harness is in the repo was not verified. 2012-era CPUs.

name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers, SFMT19937-64 (with SIMD) vs MT19937-64, measured by a third party (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) in the README of sharase/melg-64.
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s per 1e9 numbers (about 2.8x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s (about 2.3x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD: 4.2654 s and 5.6123 s (about 1.2x on both, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the melg-64 README)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; widely used reference generator (also dSFMT for doubles in the same org)
tradeoffs: Produces a different sequence from MT19937, so it is not a drop-in for std::mt19937 output. Designed for 32-bit output; for 64-bit output the high-dimensional equidistribution is worse (Harase's table gives Delta=14095 vs 0 for MELG), and dSFMT is the variant meant for doubles. 128-bit SIMD blocks with SSE2, AVX2/AVX512 (added in 1.5.2), NEON (1.5.3) and Altivec backends; README warns big-endian and Altivec are not tested. C API with the state in a struct.
caveats: The SFMT repo README has no numbers; the authors' 'about twice as fast as MT19937' claim and the MCQMC 2006 paper live on pages that could not be opened (egress blocked), so this entry rests on a third-party table from the melg-64 README, measured on 2012-era CPUs with an older gcc. The baseline is the original mt19937-64.c, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64. I did not verify that the timing harness is in the melg-64 repo.

name: apxchol
baseline: hypre BoomerAMG (CPU and GPU builds); AMGCL, RCHOL and ParAC are also in the comparison
workload: Preconditioned CG on 27 graph-Laplacian and SDDM matrices (2D/3D grids, interior-point systems, SuiteSparse and SNAP graphs) to a 1e-8 true relative residual, one right-hand side, setup plus solve time, 72 threads, with GPU rows on the Hopper GPU.
claimed_speedup: Total time (setup+solve) as competitor/apxchol ratio over paired completed matrices: CPU hypre BoomerAMG 3.267x (apxchol wins 23 of 23), BoomerAMG/cut 3.555x (25 of 25), AMGCL 1.735x (apxchol wins 10, loses 16 of 26); GPU hypre BoomerAMG 2.028x (apxchol wins 25 of 26), AMGCL 1.835x (22 of 26).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 22.1.8 with libomp for CPU rows; GCC 14.3 or Clang 22.1.8 with NVCC (GCC 14.3 host) for GPU rows; CMake Release; exact optimization flags are not listed in the summary
hardware: NVIDIA GH200 node (72-core Grace CPU + Hopper GPU) (Daint), 72 threads
tradeoffs: Specialized for graph-Laplacian and SDDM systems, not general SPD matrices. Approximate (sampled) Cholesky factor used as a PCG preconditioner, so it is iterative and stochastic. Needs a C++23 compiler and Eigen; optional CUDA path; Python and Octave/MATLAB bindings; offers an Eigen preconditioner interface. The CPU solve is memory-bandwidth bound and sensitive to thread placement across NUMA domains.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the library authors, labelled historical snapshots and not current-main measurements. AMGCL beats apxchol on 16 of 26 CPU matrices (e.g. several grid matrices in benchmarks/daint/summary.md), so the win is mainly on graph-like and interior-point systems. Pairs where hypre timed out are excluded from the ratios. 'SuiteSparse' in the benchmark tables means matrices from the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection, not the SuiteSparse library. The baselines (hypre, AMGCL) are not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc. BSD-4-Clause has an advertising clause and is not on the OSI list. The repo is young (benchmark docs dated 2026-09).

name: cuBool (GPU sparse Boolean linear algebra)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (GrB_mxm over the Boolean LOR_LAND semiring and element-wise add, CPU)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix product R = A x A and element-wise add R = A + A^2 on 10 SuiteSparse-collection graph and road matrices (62k-2.2M rows, 0.24-5.5M non-zeros); time of the operation only, data already loaded into GPU or host memory.
claimed_speedup: Matrix product time, cuBool (GPU) vs SuiteSparse (CPU): web-Google 41.8 ms vs 673.3 ms (16x, derived from page data), amazon0312 23.2 ms vs 257.6 ms (11x, derived), amazon-2008 33.3 ms vs 369.5 ms, roadNet-CA 32.0 ms vs 114.5 ms, luxembourg_osm 2.4 ms vs 3.1 ms. Element-wise add: amazon0312 11.4 ms vs 37.2 ms, web-Google 24.8 ms vs 77.5 ms.
compiler_and_flags: GCC (version not stated), CMake Release; SpBench benchmark code is public
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 3.40 GHz, 64 GB DDR4, GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB, Ubuntu 20.04

caveats: Shootout (SpBench) written by cuBool's own author in 2021 (last SpBench commit 2021-09-04): it compares a GTX 1070 GPU against SuiteSparse on a 4-core CPU, and SuiteSparse's thread count is not stated. On road networks cuBool is slower than clBool and sometimes cuSPARSE (e.g. roadNet-PA 18.1 ms vs clBool 14.2 ms) and its margin over SuiteSparse is only 1.3-3.7x there (luxembourg_osm 1.3x, roadNet-PA 3.7x). SuiteSparse here is the GraphBLAS component, not CHOLMOD or UMFPACK, so this is not a solver comparison. The README gives no compiler version or exact flags.

name: DirectLUSolvers (MultifrontalQR, SupernodalLDLT, SupernodalLU)
baseline: Eigen::SparseQR (MultifrontalQR); also Eigen::SimplicialLDLT and Eigen::SparseLU for the LDLT/LU solvers
workload: Sparse QR factorization time (single thread, best of 3, rank verification included) on 34 SuiteSparse-collection matrices that both solvers finished (Eigen was given 300 s per run), plus six matrices from the author's own application corpus.
claimed_speedup: MultifrontalQR is 5-6900x faster than Eigen::SparseQR over the 34 SuiteSparse matrices both finished, median 59x (e.g. cell2 66.6 s vs 20 ms, swang2 3182 ms vs 7.7 ms, DriftDiffusion n29841 8461 ms vs 0.52 ms). It also returns the right rank where Eigen::SparseQR does not (raefsky5: Eigen reports rank 622 of 6316).
compiler_and_flags: clang 22, -O3 at the default x86-64 ISA, CMake Release build: stated in doc/Parallelism.md for same-date benchmarks, not restated beside the QR table
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores): stated in doc/Parallelism.md for 2026-09-17 runs, not restated beside the QR table
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; 106 commits; docs dated from 2026-08-22, so under 6 weeks of public history
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 on top of Eigen, with optional METIS, oneTBB, OpenMP and MKL. Eigen-style solver interface (compute/solve/info). MultifrontalQR is rank-revealing and handles any matrix shape. The same repo also offers SupernodalLDLT (README and doc/SupernodalLDLT.md claim about 2x faster factorization than its own LU on symmetric 3D Laplacians and 6.5x vs Eigen::SimplicialLDLT at n=64000, though SimplicialLDLT wins on analyze time) and SupernodalLU/LeftRightLU, which the docs say are typically 2-3x slower and denser than Eigen::SparseLU on general matrices (but more robust on some matrices Eigen::SparseLU fails on) and about 1.5-1.8x behind MKL PARDISO.
caveats: Very new (docs dated from 2026-08), zero-star, one-author project; the GitHub description says it was implemented with Claude Code. All numbers are the author's own, from the repo's own benchmark drivers (test/bench_multifrontal_qr.cpp), and the hardware and compiler are recorded in a different doc than the QR table. Eigen::SparseQR is a weak baseline (the docs say it never permutes rows, so it has huge fill and wrong rank on badly scaled matrices); there is no comparison against SuiteSparseQR (SPQR), the real incumbent for sparse QR. Matrices where Eigen timed out are excluded from the 59x median. The LU solvers are slower than Eigen::SparseLU on general matrices, so the speedup claim applies to QR and symmetric LDLT only.
found_via: WebSearch 'sparse direct solver benchmark comparison SuiteSparse PARDISO MUMPS Eigen results' surfaced github.com/rhiestan/DirectLUSolvers; README and doc/*.md opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: SPbLA (sparse Boolean linear algebra on GPU; cuBool and clBool backends)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (CPU) plus CUSP, cuSPARSE and clSPARSE (GPU)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix multiplication M x M and element-wise addition M + M^2 on 10 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graph matrices (e.g. amazon-2008, web-Google, roadNet-CA, netherlands_osm); time in ms and memory in MB; GTX 1070 GPU versus i7-6700 CPU.
claimed_speedup: Paper: Boolean-specialized operations 'can be up to 5 times faster and consume up to 4 times less memory' than generic non-Boolean operations from CUSP or cuSPARSE. From Table II (M x M, derived from page data): cuBool 1.9 ms vs SuiteSparse 7.9 ms on matrix 0, 23.2 vs 257.6 ms on matrix 2, 33.3 vs 369.5 ms on matrix 3, 41.8 vs 673.3 ms on matrix 4 (about 4x to 16x); cuSPARSE took 4761.3 ms on matrix 4. Not uniformly faster: cuSPARSE is faster on matrix 1 (1.7 vs 2.4 ms) and CUSP/cuSPARSE are often as fast or faster for M + M^2 (Table III), where cuBool's advantage is lower memory.
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 3.40GHz, 64 GB DDR4, GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB
tradeoffs: Boolean (structure-only) matrices only; CUDA (cuBool) and OpenCL (clBool) backends plus a CPU fallback, Python bindings. Much lower peak GPU memory than the generic libraries in the paper's tables. The GPU baselines treat nonzero floats as true, so they do more work per element than a Boolean kernel.
caveats: Paper PDF text does not state its venue (it sits in a 2021/GRAPL folder of the YaccConstructor/articles repo), so peer review is unconfirmed and the tier stays C; B if the workshop venue is confirmed. The baseline comparison is GPU versus a CPU library and a Boolean kernel versus non-Boolean kernels, which the SpBench README itself calls 'not entirely fair'. Compiler and flags not stated. Public benchmark code exists at https://github.com/EgorOrachyov/SpBench (opened) but was not rerun.
found_via: GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/sparse-matrix?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars&page=2 and https://github.com/topics/graphblas; paper PDF linked from the spbla README

workload: GraphBLAS-style graph algorithms (BFS, SSSP, PageRank, triangle counting) on 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs (coAuthorsCiteseer up to road_central, indochina-2004 with 302M edges), spla on a GTX 1070 GPU versus LAGraph on the CPU of the same machine; also integrated Intel and AMD GPUs.
claimed_speedup: README log-scale bar chart of speedup over LAGraph (SuiteSparse), values read off the chart so approximate: PageRank roughly 7x to 65x, SSSP roughly 1.4x to 23x, triangle counting roughly 4x to 12x, BFS roughly 0.7x to 3.6x (slower than LAGraph on some graphs). README text also claims 'much faster than scipy or networkx' and better PageRank than Gunrock and competitive results against GraphBLAST. No exact numbers are printed.
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 3.40GHz (4 cores), 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB (also Intel HD Graphics 530, AMD GFX1036, Intel Arc A770, AMD Vega Frontier Edition)
tradeoffs: GPU-resident sparse linear algebra with C/C++ API and Python bindings (PyPI). Runs on Intel, Nvidia and AMD GPUs including integrated ones. Graph-analytics oriented (GraphBLAS semirings), not a solver library. Needs a GPU to see the gains.
caveats: Numbers exist only as a chart image (docs/stats/rq1_rel.png); the speedups here are read off the log axis. The comparison is a GTX 1070 GPU against LAGraph on a 4-core CPU, not a like-for-like device comparison. Compiler and flags are not stated; baseline runs were done by the library authors. README says the project is under heavy development and not ready for usage. BFS does not beat the baseline on every graph.
